problem: Prior LLM-robot navigation systems rely on fine-tuning or learned waypoint policies, and evaluation typically uses binary success measures that hide partial progress. It is unclear how well a purely zero-shot LLM can plan stepwise for UGVs from sensed data alone.
motivation: Semantic reasoning and adaptive planning are increasingly important for autonomous unmanned platforms (UGVs, drones). A fine-grained metric combining distance and orientation is needed to assess partial task completion in zero-shot LLM planning.
key_idea: A modular architecture feeds visual and spatial inputs to a general-purpose LLM (Gemini 2.0 Flash) that acts as a purely zero-shot, stepwise planner for UGV navigation and exploration, evaluated with a continuous distance-plus-orientation metric.
insight: The abstract reports that the LLM shows encouraging goal-directed spatial planning and partial task completion even zero-shot, but plan generation is inconsistent across models, which points to a need for task-specific adaptation or fine-tuning. The continuous metric reveals partial success that binary measures would miss. No ablation details are available from the abstract.
method: Modular architecture: integrates a general-purpose LLM with visual and spatial inputs for iterative planning to guide UGV behavior
Zero-shot stepwise planner: the LLM receives no task demonstrations and reasons only from sensed data at each step
Continuous evaluation metric: jointly measures distance and orientation, as an alternative to binary success
Simulation evaluation: navigation and exploration tasks in simulated environments with Gemini 2.0 Flash

setting.observation: visual input plus spatial/sensed data (details not given in the abstract)
setting.action_space: stepwise LLM-generated plans guiding UGV behavior (details not given)

results: Qualitatively, Gemini 2.0 Flash shows encouraging goal-directed spatial planning and partial task completion in zero-shot navigation and exploration tasks. Plan generation is inconsistent across models. No numeric results are available in the abstract.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation on a single foundational LLM as the primary model, with no reported real-robot validation
Zero-shot performance is only partial, so task-specific adaptation is needed
